name: Discontent and Grumbling

counsel.text: Discontent is a fretting humour, which dries the brains, wastes the spirits, corrodes and eats out the comfort of life; discontent makes a man that he doth not enjoy what he doth possess. A drop or two of vinegar will sour a whole glass of wine.
counsel.author: Thomas Watson
counsel.source: The Art of Divine Contentment, ch. 8

counsel.text: These do secretly tax the wisdom of God, that he hath not screwed them up in their condition a peg higher.
counsel.author: Thomas Watson
counsel.source: The Art of Divine Contentment, ch. 9

counsel.text: Learn quietly to submit to divine providence. Do not murmur at things that are ordered by divine wisdom. We may no more find fault with the works of providence than we may with the works of creation. It is a sin as much to quarrel with God's providence as to deny his providence.
counsel.author: Thomas Watson
counsel.source: A Body of Divinity, the providence of God

counsel.text: Rise mightily against the first actings of thy distemper, its first conceptions; suffer it not to get the least ground. Do not say, "Thus far it shall go, and no farther." If it have allowance for one step, it will take another. It is impossible to fix bounds to sin.
counsel.author: John Owen
counsel.source: Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers, ch. 11

counsel.text: Get an humble spirit. The humble man is the contented man; if his estate be low, his heart is lower than his estate, therefore be content. If his esteem in the world be low, he that is little in his own eyes will not be much troubled to be little in the eyes of others.
counsel.author: Thomas Watson
counsel.source: The Art of Divine Contentment, ch. 14

counsel.text: When the heart is once won to rest in God, to repose himself on him, he will assuredly satisfy it. He will never be as water that fails; nor hath he said at any time to the seed of Jacob, "Seek ye my face in vain." If Christ be chosen for the foundation of our supply, he will not fail us.
counsel.author: John Owen
counsel.source: Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers, ch. 14

prayers.title: A prayer of confession
prayers.text: Wise and sovereign Father, you work all things according to the counsel of your will, and you have set my lot in love. I come in the name of your Son. I confess that I have been discontented. I have grumbled about my circumstances as if you had made a mistake. I have complained in my heart and with my mouth, and I have forgotten your many mercies. Like Israel in the wilderness, I have murmured against your goodness while you fed me every day. This is unbelief and ingratitude. Forgive me, Lord. Christ endured the cross for the joy set before him, and he learned obedience through what he suffered. For his sake pardon me. Holy Spirit, put this grumbling to death, and teach me, as you taught Paul, the secret of being content in plenty and in want. I thank you that your grace is sufficient for me, and that all things work together for good for those who love you. In Jesus' name. Amen.

prayers.title: When I start to complain
prayers.text: Lord, I feel the complaint rising in me again. I bring it to you instead of letting it run. You have not wronged me. You are good, and your way is perfect even when I cannot understand it. Help me count your mercies, beginning now. Teach me to say, The Lord gave and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord. Lord Jesus, you had nowhere to lay your head, and you did not grumble. Spirit of God, give me a thankful heart. Amen.

prayers.title: For a thankful heart
prayers.text: Father, you have given me far more than I deserve: life and breath, daily bread, the gospel, your Son, your Spirit, and your church. Forgive me for overlooking so much. Open my eyes to your daily kindness. Make me content with what I have, because you have said that you will never leave me nor forsake me. Teach me to give thanks in all circumstances, for this is your will for me in Christ Jesus. Let my mouth be full of praise instead of complaint, so that others may see your goodness. Through Jesus Christ. Amen.

examinationQuestions: What did you complain about today, out loud or in your heart, and what did that complaint say about how you see God's wisdom and care?
What were you wanting when the discontent rose up: comfort, honor, ease, or something another person has?
Which of God's mercies to you today did you overlook or take for granted?
Has your grumbling made the load heavier for those around you, at home, at work, or in your church?
Is there a place where God has set you that you are fighting instead of serving in?
Are you more troubled by your hard circumstances or by the sin in your own heart?
fleeActions: Stop and say out loud three specific mercies God has given you today, and thank him for each one.
If a complaint is on your lips, leave it unspoken for now. Take it to God in honest prayer before you speak of it to anyone.
Do one task you have been resenting, and do it carefully, as service to Christ.
Read Philippians 4:4-13 slowly, and ask God to teach you what Paul learned.
Message a brother or sister in your church and ask them to pray that you would be content. Then ask how you can pray for them.
Write a short note of thanks to someone God has used for your good, and send it today.

afterFallReadings.text: Every man is complaining that his estate is no better, though he seldom complains that his heart is no better.
afterFallReadings.author: Thomas Watson
afterFallReadings.source: The Art of Divine Contentment, ch. 9

afterFallReadings.text: Hast thou not often been ready to conclude thyself, that it was utterly impossible that he should bear any longer with thee; that he would cast thee off, and be gracious no more; that all his forbearance was exhausted, and hell and wrath was even ready prepared for thee? and yet, above all thy expectation, he hath returned with visitations of love.
afterFallReadings.author: John Owen
afterFallReadings.source: Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers, ch. 11

afterFallReadings.text: If God be ours, whatever we want in the creature, is infinitely made up in him. Do I want bread? I have Christ the bread of life. Am I under defilement? his blood is like the trees of the sanctuary; not only for meat, but medicine.
afterFallReadings.author: Thomas Watson
afterFallReadings.source: The Art of Divine Contentment, ch. 14
